This is an update to [this discussion](https://voat.co/v/Bicycling/comments/924590) I posted a while back. Both discussions may be of interest to those who are considering a folding bicycle and are worried about things like ride quality and carrying capacity.

So I finally got a chance to ***really*** put the bike to work. After being confident about having the bike set up to haul a decent amount of weight, I went grocery shopping and was able to load it up with approximately 35 pounds (!!!!!!) of stuff, and yes I did actually weigh it all. So just to be clear, I managed to put all of those 35 pounds on the folding bike itself without having to resort to using a backpack. ???????? This just goes to show you that folding bikes can be used to haul cargo too.

So how well did the bike handle it? Pretty well. The ride was much smoother and stiffer than I expected, accelerating from a stop was not much of an issue, and shifting handled just fine with the added pedal force needed to move the bike. But I should also point out that the 20" tires on the bike are 1.75 inches wide, which equates to a much smoother ride than the skinnier tires some people may be used to (wider and lower pressure tires act to cushion shock and vibration). That said, the bike did like to behave a bit bouncier with all that extra weight on it whenever I'd go over even the slightest bumps, but I guess that's to be expected when hanging that much weight on such a small bike. Thankfully small wheels are stronger than large ones, and I have a good saddle that flexes, meaning my butt wasn't subjected to punishment from the bouncing.

Now to hill climbing. First off, I climb hills on my bikes all the time. I'm used to it. But with 35 extra pounds on the bike and only 7 gears (the folding bike I got has only one chain ring), it's going to be a bit harder obviously. The wind also conspired against me. On the way back home, I was facing into a nasty headwind. So I was doing a pretty good amount of climbing while having to combat that headwind and hauling the extra weight, all with only 7 gears. The bike did just fine, though. At no point did I feel the need to stand up, but I did get some good cardio out of it! I won't say it was easy, but I will say that folding bikes have small wheels, which I do think must help on the climbs.

I should note at this point that I consider myself to be a reasonably fit and relatively light weight cyclist, so of course YMMV. If you don't think you're in that good of a shape, you're significantly heavier than me, and you expect to be facing hills or strong wind, you might want to consider a folder with more gears for climbing. That said, if you're fit and you don't weigh too much, you may find that those extra gears aren't as necessary as you'd think.

I hope this was of interest and of some use to people thinking about getting a folder. Oh, and one more thing: as long as you get a good-looking bike, you won't look silly riding it . I've read some people are actually concerned about looking stupid on a folding bike. I've caught sideways glances at my reflection while riding, and I think I look fairly normal, but the bike I got also looks pretty nice, so that helps. Like most people around here, I ride in street clothes. Someone in lycra might look ridiculous on a folder. I personally have been getting compliments on the bike ever since I got it, and people often remark to eachother from within earshot of me about how cool they think it is. Maybe it's not the same everywhere, but that's how people have been reacting where I live.

Again, YMMV.
